abstract: (Associate Member): I don't wish to anticipate Mr. Whimster's reply, but I should like to point out that on the question of pressure testing I think some members are under a misapprehension as to what “2ë times working pressure “ signifies in the paper. Mr. Aikman, for one, has stated that it seems unnecessarily high. Well, as far as three-phase apparatus is concerned, the test is usually at a pressure of 2ë, times working pressure to neutral, and not 2ë times the rated pressure between the lines. That is to say current or pressure transformers, for instance, to be used on a 10,000 volt system are tested to about 14,000 volts and not to 25,000 volts. This is applied between the primary windings and earthed secondary windings and is strictly speaking 2ë times the pressure between these points under normal conditions assuming the neutral of the system to be earthed in some form or other as is usually done with high tension systems.

abstract: (Member of Council): I read Mr. Elsdon-Dew's paper with great interest. A good many years ago I was connected with what is now one of the latest water power schemes in the Transvaal, and notice quite a lot of improvements in them ; more especially in the governing of the Turbines. The governor we had was a nigger on the wheel, and it was not a very effective one. Wo had no trouble with lightning for we had cables. We had quite a lot of trouble though, due to the racing of the turbines; for instance, the niggers would open the valve instead of shutting it. We also had quite a lot of trouble, as we were not allowed to parallel the machines — the old type two-phase machines — until one of the shifts men happened to come on duty a little bit drunk and by accident he paralleled them, and when we went down to relieve him in the morning we fouhd all the switches in position. When we asked him what was the matter, he said “I do not know.” We said “Did you not hear anything?” He said “I heard the belts slip.” We used to run them in parallel afterwards very successfully.

abstract: I notice in Mr. Gould's paper he mentions single-stroke bells. I think anybody who uses single-stroke bells in mining work is sacrificing his safety, for the simple reason that a single-stroke bell is not reliable, inasmuch as yon can get enough leakage, that when you give one signal the cnrrent will hold the armature of the bell up and won't release it again; a man goes to give a second signal and it won't work. I have had several years' experience with them and I still find them absolutely unreliable if yon happen to get any leakag-e at all. I would like Mr. Gould to tell us, when he is running bells off accumulators, whether he has reversed his current at all, that is, changed his positive and negative wires. Occasionally I find that a very great help indeed. The positive wire drives out and the negative absorbs the moisture; and if you are continually reversing you keep yonr leads dry.

articleTitle: Thunderstorms
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Mr. G. V. Adendorff then delivered it lecture on the subject of thunderstorms. He gave a brief account of the early investigations of such pioneers as Franklin, and dealt with the determining factors as to how thunderstorms are formed, such as the clouds, the atmosphere and atmospheric electrification. The formation of clouds and the electrification of the atmosphere was lucidly explained by the lecturer, and the various points raised in connection with the various directions of the winds associated with thunderstorms was followed with keen interest by the members of the Institute. The lecturer then dealt with various phenomena connected with the actual electrification of clouds and explained how by the coalescence of electrified drops of moisture uniting in rain drops, and ultimately a cloud, a very large potential is attained. Having led up to the actual electrification of clouds, the peculiar vagaries and different kinds of lightning were then discussed. By a series of most interesting experiments which Mr. Adendorff had arranged, with considerable trouble, the effect of points dissipating a static charge and their protective effect was most beautifully shewn by means of the Wemshurst machine. The lecturer also pointed out the difference between the lightning discharges resulting from the breaking down of the atmosphere through electric stress in the case of steady electric strain and sudden or impulsive stress, and the lecturer explained the circumstances of the existence of these two conditions. The lecturer was highly successful with his experiments, and in the case of the impulsive stroke it was shewn clearly how the stroke took the path of least resistance, which was generally the highest object, no matter whether that object was pointed or otherwise ; and that points which proved protective against the lightning stroke from a steady stress, were ineffective in protecting the highest object from being struck by the impulsive lightning stroke. This was a point which appealed very strongly to the members of the Institute as bearing upon the important subject of lightning protection, which was finally dealt with by the lecturer, thus terminating what was undoubtedly a highly interesting and beneficial lecture.

articleTitle: Electrification of railways
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: (Associate Member): The thanks of this Institute are due to Professor Buchanan for bis interesting paper on this subject. My idea in these few notes this evening is not so much to criticise the author's paper as to endeavour to express a few thoughts that have occurred to me in reading the progress of the electrification of railways in various parts of the world. Early in the paper disappointment is expressed at the tardiness with which electricity has been applied to railways; this remark is especially brought home to us in this country when we remember that Africa is the only continent in which no rail way electrification or conversion schemes are actually in existence. The author rightly hits the mark when he says that possibly the authorities who postpone investigation of the subject until electricians agree upon the best system, have a valid reason for their conservatism. It is now for the Electrical Engineering profession to make out their case for the electrification of railways, and then for local conditions to prove the deciding factors in the choice of systems. The Railway Gazcttry in discussing this aspect of the question, says : “ Too much stress must not be laid on the disadvantages of lack of uniformity in the system of electrification adopted by different railways. …. It is better to put up with these disadvantages of electric working than to wai t until the best system is discovered or to put difficulties in the way of its ever being discovered by tying all railways down to rigid uniformity.” Nevertheless, in a country situated as we are 6,000 miles from manufacturing centres, it is well that before any electrification takes place the various schemes that have been worked out in other parts of the world should be well studied and considered so that when the time does come for the consideration of railway electrification in this country, our profession will be fully conversant with the difficulties that have been found in other schemes.

abstract: The President: Before calling on Prof. Buchanan to reply to the discussion on his paper, I have great pleasure in extending a hearty welcome to Mr. Mills, Electrical Engineer to the South African Railways. I understand he proposes to say a few words on this paper. As you are aware, gentlemen, the subject of the electrification of railways is dealt with by Mr. Hoy, the General Manager of the South African Railways, in his report of last year. He thinks the time is now ripe for a report to be made on this matter dealing with South Africa generally, and, as it is a very important matter, I hope some result will come of it for the benefit of engineering generally. Prof. Buchanan is to be congratulated on having brought forward this question. I was to have contributed to the paper, but, unfortunately, I have not been able to find the time. My intention bad been to touch on that very much wider application of electricity : the supply of electrical power hand-in-hand with the electrification of railways throughout the country. I can safely predict that this side of the question will also have to be considered when electrification is being discussed. I feel certain that the linking up of the water powers now running to waste will assist in this greater scheme — the supply of cheap power for railways, irrigation, manufactures, and every other expansion in this country ; this is possible now as we know, for the way electrical supply has recently increased is an assurance that this is the direction of progress. I now have very much pleasure in calling on Mr. Mills.

I have had the pleasure of reading the full notes that were taken at the meeting, and Mr. Adendorff has summarised so very conclusively and so well all the different points connected with thunderstorms that it is instructive to everyone dealing with power schemes to realise all the different stresses set up in power lines, not only from the direct strokes, but also from the different lightning effects that Mr. Adendorff described so well. It is rather a fascinating subject to follow up. Mr. Adendorff's lecture will assist everyone who has to deal with the question of lightning arrestors on power lines and it will enable them to deal with the subject in an easier manner than previously. abstract: (Past president): There are one or two remarks which I might make in a genend way on the paper. One particular point that I thought might be useful, but which has not been mentioned by Mr. Whimster, is the very practical ami accurate method, and a cheap one, of using for balance loads only a single meter. I know on a mine with which I was once concerned — where we bad a great many groups of three-phase motors and single motors that required metering — we found that a good, reliable and satisfactory way of measuring was by means of a single-phase meter where in most cases you can get at the neutral point, or you can make an artificial neutral. We found it was an extremely accurate method of three-phase measurement. It strikes me very forcibly that in Mr. Whimster's diagram, showing the stop-watch testing apparatus, a switch is required very badly in the battery circuit, unless yon limit your-self entirely to three-seconds testing, which I do not think is long enough. From a good deal of stop-watch experience, I think also he is asstiming a good deal in saying that in the case of starting and stopping it is possible to make an error of only one centimeter. It is rather small : because I know the timing of your pendulum is something terrible. I know in one instance where we were using for timing a pendulum that was a seconds pendulum; inside the battery we inserted an ordinary cyclometer moved by an electro-magnet. You could start that by a press-button and ordinary bell-push, and yon could move that for five minutes if you liked and stop it by simply a press button short-circuiting arrangement. That seemed to me a very satisfactory way. In the early part of his paper, he says on page 289 of the December “Transactions“: “The Electriad Testing Department should have under its control the arranging and carrying out of such work, and in the case of routine work the responsibility for the satisfactory working of all electrical gear requiring periodical testing should rest with that department.” That, I think, is a very strong point, because the people operating any instruments should only be concerned with the actual operation in practice. I was not prepared this evening for a detailed discussion, but I hope to give a written contribution at a later date.

articleTitle: Notes on mine signalling systems
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In a mining district such as ours, where a large proportion of the engineers are either directly or indirectly connected with the mines, it is surprising to note how little the subject of signalling in the mines has been dealt with in technical papers. Perhaps it is because the importance of the signalling system is not realised to the extent it deserves. The development of railways would have been considerably retarded without the telegraph, and I need add no words to convince you that the same would apply to deep level mines if signalling arrangements had not been devised. The method most commonly used for signalling in mines before electrical signalling became more general, consisted of a knocker operated by a flexible wire rope, the “ knocker-line.” As this arrangement can be installed by the miner or timberman and can be kept in order by them, the mining men here “ hung on “ to this system as long as possible. It certainly has the advantage of being simple and, if properly installed, it is reliable within certain limits of length of shafts, and last, but not least, it keeps the electrician out of the shaft, which is a consideration ! However, since the Government mining regulations require two systems of signalling, one of which can be operated only by an authorised person, mining men here had to resort to electric signalling. The system most commonly used on these fields is shown in its simplest form on Fig. 1. This shows the arrangement for two compartments of a shaft, and it will be seen that four wires are required to be led down the shaft. It is now the general practice to use rubber-insulated, lead-covered and wire-armoured cable for this purpose, with suitable “Tee “ boxes at the various stations. The general rule is to use 7/20 s.w.g. wire, although 7/18 s.w.g. is used on some properties. In come cases the battery wires are heavier than the compartment wires, With regard to the insulation, I have not. heard of any paper-insulated cable being installed for this purpose on the Rand, but, provided proper tee boxes and end boxes are installed, I do not see any reason why paper cable should not be used ; but perhaps the discussion, which I trust will be a lively one, Will give me your opinion in this respect. If you take measurements of the voltages obtaining at the various points of your bell system, you will find that the drops are comparatively high and that voltages occur where they are not expected and where they may become troublesome. Looking at Fig. 1 : if LP9 pull is operated, the voltage at the terminal of the LBS bell will be the lowest, and it will also be found that a potential difference exists at some of the right compartment hells ; to get clear on this latter point particularly, I rigged up a number of bells as per Fig. 1, using resistance wire for the connections between the various stations, thus getting as near as possible to actual working conditions. Between the surface bells and the bells at the first level, resistance wires of 1-14 ohms each are connected, being the equivalent resistance of 1,000 ft. of 7/20 s.w.g. copper conductor. Between the other levels each connecting wire has a resistance of 0·342 ohms, being the equivalent of 300 feet of 7/20 s.w.g. cable. We thus have reproduced the conditions which would prevail on a four-wire signalling system with one bell on the surface for each of the two compartments, one each at No. 1 level, 1,000 feet below the surface, and one bell for each compartment at each subsequent level, each level being 300 feet apart (as far as the cable run is concerned). The batteries should be connected direct on to the two battery leads PC and BC in Fig. 1. If a switch is used, it should be locked to prevent unauthorised persons from disconnecting the battery. Where primary cells are employed the internal resistance of the cells will limit the amount of current on a short circuit occurring and thus prevent anything happening to the connections, but where accumulators are used, unless these be of a type that can stand short circuiting, I consider that some current limiting device should be employed in preference to fuses, and a properly selected iron wire resistance will meet the case, which on a short circuit would heat up and increase in resistance. Coming now to the pulls, there are a large number of different designs on the market and a good many different designs are in actual use on the Rand. I have not seen a pull yet which could not be improved in some way or another. Generally speaking, the bell pulls on the Rand can be divided into two classes : the side lever and the plunger type. The experience with the side lever is that the knife which makes contact by bridging the two contact springs wears badly, and after a while is apt to give two signals for one pull at the lever. The plunger type pull is theoretically of wrong design, as its action is that of an air-pump and is therefore liable to become dirty inside and corrode at the contacts, but in practice, however, this pull is generally found to be satisfactory. I have laid on the table a pull which was made, to my design. This pull is intended to work in oil and you will notice has a quick make and break to ensure positive signals. As the law requires two distinct systems of signalling to be installed in each shaft, one which can be operated by an authorised person only and the other by anyone from any level in the shaft, numerous lock bell pulls have been designed of late to meet this requirement. Some mines prefer ordinary bell pulls fitted in locked-up boxes which can be opened only by the properly authorised person.
